neighbours.label: A verb that repeats an expression used just before (No, it makes sense to...; ends up where it should end up), vs the same idioms used once
fire: Does it pay to wait for a sale? Honestly, it pays to buy when you need it.
The plan was going to fall apart, and fall apart it did within a week.
Who told you to leave early? Nobody told me to leave; I just went.
They said the drug would change everything, and it did change everything for patients.
Is the old bridge still standing? Yes, it still stands after two hundred years.
He wanted to win the race, and he did win the race in record time.
Can you keep a secret? I can keep a secret better than anyone.
The store says it will close at nine, but it never closes before ten.
quiet: Waiting for a sale is often smart if you can plan your purchases ahead.
The plan was fragile, and the team abandoned it within a week.
My manager let me go home early because the office was quiet.
Doctors hoped the drug would help, and many patients felt better.
The old bridge across the river was built two hundred years ago.
He trained for months, and the race went well for him in the end.
My sister is very good with secrets and never gossips.
The store opens at eight on weekdays and later on Sundays.

predictions: Fire 0.3-0.8 on the verb of the repeated phrase; near misses with the idiom used once under 0.1.
short: repeated verb of an echoed phrase
notes: Card top examples repeat a phrase just used: 'No, it makes sense to call that child', 'I do not bid thee call' after 'Who bids thee call', 'It was out of date' after 'it is out of date', 'Engag'd' twice. Probe: echoed 'makes sense' 0.775, echoed 'end up' 0.587; single-use 'give them up' 0.008, 'didn't make a difference' 0.029, 'makes bread' 0.003.
